model.iron_lamination: TRANSVERSE-ISOTROPIC: the 2D materials' homogenised curve in the sheet plane, the insulation-limited series average across the stack (solver.axial_mu, k_f = 0.92 from the same material the 2D curve was laminated with).  Measured mu_r: stator 742 in plane / 12.3 axial, rotor 162 / 11.7.

two_d.solver: fem_solver_2d weak form (P2, full ring, static3d cross-section mirrored), CONVERGED Picard — ref2d.solve_2d_reference_converged
two_d.relaxation: geometric in log(mu), adaptive, constitutive-residual stop

shipped_relaxation.verdict: NOT a solution: its Picard limit-cycles at a constitutive residual of ~0.8 and breaks the machine's exact anti-periodicity by 3 %. Kept for the before/after only.

mesh_errors.3D_basis: three cross-sections at the saturated point, 1.46937 / 1.47227 / 1.46943 T (isotropic model, round 3), and two formulations 0.6 % apart on one mesh
mesh_errors.2D_basis: five cross-sections from 4 025 to 12 769 triangles with the converged relaxation: 1.52010 / 1.51951 / 1.51868 / 1.51528 / 1.51542 T (0.3 % total spread, the two finest 0.01 % apart)

demag.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising; at I=0 the END elements sit at a LESS negative H than the mid-plane ones because the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet
demag.measured_on: the ISOTROPIC iron (round 3) — the exposure SHIFT between the end and mid slices is a ratio inside the magnets, which the iron anisotropy moves far less than it moves the axial spill, but it has not been re-measured.

bracket.note: phi=0 forces B normal to the truncation surface, dphi/dn=0 forces it tangential; the true answer lies between, so the spread is a BOUND on the truncation error, not an estimate
bracket.measured_on: the ISOTROPIC iron at max_iter 45 (round 3) — not re-run for the laminated model.  It bounds the TRUNCATION error only (0.008 % on k_flux_self), and nothing about the air box changed, so it is carried over rather than re-spent; the lamination change it does NOT cover is quoted separately below and is 200x larger.

_schema._doc: 3D end-effect passport for ONE machine (magnet-only, I = 0).

fields.geometry_fingerprint: routes.simulation._geometry_fingerprint of the geometry this was solved for; a passport whose fingerprint does not match the active design describes a different motor and must be ignored.
fields.machine: slots/poles/radii/stack/materials actually solved, mm and T.
fields.model: sector angle, periodicity sign, element order, air box, mesh sizes, z levels — everything needed to reproduce.
fields.k_flux: axial mean of the gap fundamental over the stack, divided by the 2D fundamental. Multiply a 2D flux linkage / EMF / back-EMF constant by this.
fields.k_flux_self: same average divided by the 3D MID-PLANE value: the pure end effect, with any 2D-vs-3D modelling difference removed. k_flux = k_flux_self * (B1_3D_mid / B1_2D).
fields.spill_profile: z stations (m, and z/(L/2)) with B1(z) in T and B1(z)/B1(0). Stations beyond z/(L/2) = 1 are OUTSIDE the iron and are the fringing tail, not stack flux.
fields.two_d: the 2D reference: solver, mesh, B1 and the 3D-mid/2D ratio.
fields.demag: H.Mhat per axial magnet slice; negative is demagnetising.
fields.bracket: Dirichlet vs Neumann outer boundary at the chosen box — a CONSERVATIVE bound on the truncation error, not an estimate.
fields.solves: dofs, elements, wall time and Picard state of every solve.
fields.consistency_investigation: why the two_d check fails, measured — one block per round of investigation, each naming what was ruled out and how. Read this before trusting or re-deriving k_flux.

consistency_investigation._doc: Why the 3D-vs-2D check failed, measured, in four rounds: the magnet law (fixed, 40b7de7), the mu_r ladder (the cross-section mesh, not the formulation), the 8 % that survived rounds 1-3, and round 4 — the 2D solver's saturation state was never a solution, and the 3D iron was missing an anisotropy 2D cannot have.
consistency_investigation.status: RESOLVED — 3D mid-plane and 2D now agree to 0.80 % on the same cross-section (tolerance 2 %), k_flux is usable

round_1_magnet_law.finding: fem_solver_2d assembled M where the law B = mu0*mu_r*H + mu0*M demands M/mu_rec; 2D magnets were 5 % strong

round_2_the_mu_r_ladder.the_hypothesis: the residual grew with mu_r and vanished without iron, which is the signature of the TOTAL scalar potential cancelling inside high-mu iron (B = -mu grad phi, large times small)

test_a_exact_iron_benchmark.what: magnetised sphere inside a concentric iron shell, which has a CLOSED-FORM solution at every mu_r (static3d.exact.sphere_in_shell_B).  One mesh, 56680 tets; three formulations; mu_r = 1 .. 1e6.  Reproduce with: python -m motor_ai_sim.simulation.static3d.benchmarks --ladder
test_a_exact_iron_benchmark.conclusion: every error is FLAT in mu_r (spread x1.11 to x1.16 over mu_r = 10..1e6), and the total scalar potential at P2 is the MOST accurate of the three in the iron — about 2.7x better than the lowest order edge element on the same mesh.  The hypothesis had the two scalar potentials swapped: it is the REDUCED potential that cancels in iron, which is why the TOTAL potential is the standard cure for it.

test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.what: the machine itself, linear iron at mu_r = 4625, 3D scalar P2 sector vs the 2D solver on the SAME cross-section, refining the in-plane element size of the SOLID regions and nothing else
test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.conclusion: the residual converges MONOTONICALLY to zero with cross-section refinement — both legs converge onto B1 = 0.0576 T — so it is discretisation error, and it is in the thin rotor bridges.  The passport above was solved at h_solid = 1.2 mm, between the first two rungs.
test_b_the_residual_is_the_CROSS_SECTION.why_it_looks_like_a_mu_r_effect: with LINEAR iron at mu_r >~ 200 the un-saturated rotor bridges short ~96 % of the magnet flux, so the gap fundamental is the small remainder and is proportional to 1/mu_r (d ln B1 / d ln mu_r = -0.91 measured between mu_r = 1000 and 4625).  A sub-percent error in the bridge reluctance is then a several-percent error in B1.  The amplifier is the BRIDGE SHUNT, not the potential — and it is an artefact of running the iron linear: the real machine saturates those bridges (mu_r ~ 5) and B1 is 1.47 T, not 0.058 T.

test_c_it_is_not_an_end_effect.what: the same linear mu_r = 4625 case at 1x, 2x and 4x the stack, against the same 2D reference
test_c_it_is_not_an_end_effect.conclusion: flat — a finite-stack effect would close as the stack grows, and this does not

test_d_the_nedelec_formulation_does_not_.what: the same ladder solved in the A-formulation on Nedelec edge elements (static3d/nedelec.py), same mesh, same Region list, same post-processing
test_d_the_nedelec_formulation_does_not_.conclusion: the edge element's residual grows with mu_r too, in the OPPOSITE direction, and the three formulations straddle the 2D answer by 20 % at mu_r = 4625.  That is what a mesh-limited quantity looks like, and it settles the Stage-B question: the vector potential is not a fix for this, and on the same mesh the lowest-order edge element is the least accurate of the three.

round_3_what_is_left.the_number: with the magnet law fixed and both models converged, the NONLINEAR machine's 3D mid-plane gap fundamental sits about 8 % above the 2D solver's on the same cross-section: 3D 1.470 T +/- 0.2 %, 2D 1.36 T +/- 1 %
known_contributions: Picard noise: the 2D leg moves about 1 % between sweep counts on a fixed mesh (and 3.1 % on the passport's own cross-section, where 16 sweeps is an outlier at 1.328 T against a 1.355-1.369 T cluster); the 3D leg stops at its 45-sweep cap with a constitutive residual of 6.4e-3 against a 3e-3 tolerance. That is noise ON the residual, not the residual.

the two Picards do not agree on what |B| an element has: fem_solver_2d averages |B| over the quadrature points, static3d.solver takes |mean B|, and on a saturating bridge those are different points on the same curve. Note the SIGN before blaming it: the 2D convention reads the LARGER |B|, so it saturates the bridges more, shunts less and should read HIGHER — the opposite of what is measured. Reconciling it would widen the gap, not close it, which is exactly why it has to be reconciled before anything else is concluded.

cross-section resolution is NOT it at this operating point: refining h_solid from 1.5 to 0.6 mm moves the 3D leg by 0.2 % and leaves the ratio at 1.077 — the saturated bridges do not amplify a mesh error the way the linear ladder's un-saturated ones did
next_steps: make the two element-|B| definitions the same and re-measure — it is the one KNOWN difference in how the two models read the same B-H curve, and its sign says the true gap is wider than 8 %
converge both Picards (raise the 3D cap; give fem_solver_2d the adaptive geometric damping and constitutive-residual test static3d already uses) so the +/-1 % noise stops masking the next effect
then compare something that is NOT the gap fundamental — magnet flux and bridge flux at the mid-plane — to say WHERE the two models put the flux differently, which the gap harmonic alone cannot

nonlinear_vs_cross_section_resolution._doc: the SAME nonlinear machine at three cross-section resolutions, 3D scalar P2 sector vs the 2D solver on that same cross-section — the round-2 refinement test, repeated at the real (saturated) operating point
nonlinear_vs_cross_section_resolution.note: this does NOT converge the way the linear ladder did, and the reason is visible in the columns: the 3D leg is steady to 0.2 % across the three meshes (1.46937 / 1.47227 / 1.46943 T) while the 2D leg wanders by 1.8 % (1.36093 / 1.38567 / 1.36439 T) and the ratio wanders with it.  A saturated bridge does not amplify a mesh error the way an un-saturated one does, so at the REAL operating point the mesh is no longer the story: the 3D answer is converged, and what is left is a genuine ~7-8 % model disagreement with 1-3 % of 2D Picard limit-cycle noise on top

three_way_on_a_coarser_cross_section._doc: the same nonlinear machine solved three ways on ONE mesh (h_gap 0.45 mm, h_solid 1.5 mm, box 60.0 mm, 108675 tets) with the 2D leg on the same cross-section — the three-way the Nedelec spike was commissioned to produce

the_2d_leg_is_converged_too._doc: the 2D reference alone, on four cross-sections and at four Picard sweep counts each — because 'the other model is under-resolved' is the easiest thing to assume and the cheapest thing to check
the_2d_leg_is_converged_too.conclusion: 1.36 T +/- 1 %, with no trend in either direction — the 2D leg is mesh-converged and its Picard noise is about 1 %.  Both models are therefore converged, roughly 8 % apart, and that gap is a MODEL difference, not a numerical one.

superseded_blocks.linear_iron_3D_over_2D_by_mu_r: the ladder recorded here in the first pass (0.9151 at mu_r = 4625 up to 0.9451 at mu_r = 10) was taken with the pre-40b7de7 2D leg; multiplied by the 4.94 % magnet-law factor it becomes the -3.9 % to -0.8 % ladder the round-2 tests above explain and remove
superseded_blocks.linear_note: the original conclusion — 'the offset does not vanish as mu_r falls, so it is NOT the total scalar potential's cancellation' — was right about the cancellation and wrong about the reason: the offset at low mu_r was the magnet law, and the growth with mu_r was the bridge-shunt amplification of the mesh error

suspect_1_lamination_homogenisation_PRIM.hypothesis: the 3D iron eats the RAW steel curve while the 2D iron eats the k_f-homogenised one, so 3D iron is 1/0.92 more permeable and the iron-shunted magnet circuit lands the gap flux HIGHER

measurement.how: static3d.motor_geometry builds its regions from the SAME fem_solver_2d.build_materials call the 2D leg uses; the curves were compared point by point
measurement.note: the raw-vs-laminated gap is 0.15 T, so the null result is a measurement, not a tolerance artefact

suspect_2_bh_interpolation.verdict: FALSIFIED — there is only one implementation
suspect_2_bh_interpolation.measurement: both legs call field_ops._mu_r_from_bh_vec on the same curve object (H(B) linear in B, differential mu0 above the last sample); static3d.solver imports it from field_ops precisely so it cannot drift

suspect_3_the_magnets.measurement: the 2D magnets carry a 2nd-quadrant demag curve, but solve_magnetostatics_fem's Picard updates DOM_STATOR, DOM_ROTOR and DOM_SHAFT only — both models hold the magnets linear at mu_rec = 1.05

suspect_4_the_2d_picard_fixed_point_CAUS.verdict: CONFIRMED — the whole of the 8 %, and 4 % more
suspect_4_the_2d_picard_fixed_point_CAUS.what_is_wrong: fem_solver_2d relaxes the B-H fixed point arithmetically in nu with a fixed 0.5 damping and stops when the STEP is small.  On a saturating spoke rotor it limit-cycles: the state it returns violates the curve it was handed by ~80 %.

shipped_relaxation.why_the_harmonics_are_a_test: 7 poles per 180 deg sector makes the machine EXACTLY anti-periodic, so B_r(theta+pi) = -B_r(theta) and every EVEN harmonic of B_r is zero in any solution.  The nonlinear problem is monotone and has exactly one solution, so 3 % of even harmonic is 3 % of field that is not physics.

converged_relaxation.how: same weak form, same mesh, same materials, same curve — geometric damping in log(mu), adaptive step, stopped on the constitutive residual || |B|(nu_curve - nu_used) || / || |B| nu_curve ||
converged_relaxation.validated: bit-identical to solve_magnetostatics_fem at equal permeability (zero nonlinear sweeps), pinned by tests/test_static3d_stage_a.py::test_the_converged_2d_leg_is_the_shipped_weak_form
converged_relaxation.conclusion: 1.515-1.520 T across five cross-sections (0.3 % spread, the two finest 0.01 % apart), anti-periodicity restored to 0.03 %, and 11-12 % above the shipped relaxation on the same meshes

suspect_5_the_mu_field_transplant.verdict: INCONCLUSIVE BY CONSTRUCTION — recorded so it is not re-run
suspect_5_the_mu_field_transplant.why: it transplanted the 2D limit cycle's permeability, not a fixed point's (its two anti-periodic copies differ by 90 % in the mean).  The control failed too: quantising mu into 48 log bins (max 10 % error) moved the 2D gap fundamental by +32 % — which is its own result, the saturated bridge shunt is stiff enough that a few percent of mu is tens of percent of gap flux, and that is why a badly relaxed Picard lands so far out.

round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy._doc: A physics gap this comparison surfaced, not a tuning knob: across a stack, steel and insulation are in SERIES, so mu_z is insulation-limited at mu0/(1-k_f) = 12.5 mu0 against an in-plane 4600.  A 2D model cannot represent it at all; the 3D model was solving a solid block, which let end-region flux cross the laminations as if they were steel.

one_mesh_one_flag.cross_section: h_gap 0.35, h_solid 1.2, box 160 mm, P2, 90-sweep cap

round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.RE_QUOTE: k_flux_self moves from 0.97503 to 0.95944, i.e. -1.6 %, which is 200x the truncation bracket (0.008 %) this passport quotes as its error bar.  The end-effect answer for the 40 mm is therefore materially different from every previous revision, and it is a physics correction, not a fit: blocking the axial path through the laminations makes MORE of the magnet flux reach the gap at the mid-plane (+2.5 %) and LESS of it survive toward the ends (-1.6 % on the axial mean).
round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.and_it_closes_the_check: with solid iron the 3D mid-plane sits 3.24 % below the converged 2D leg; with the stack's own anisotropy, 0.80 % — inside the 2 % agreement tolerance, so k_flux is usable for the first time
round_4_the_lamination_anisotropy.pinned_by: tests/test_static3d_stage_a.py::test_axial_permeability_of_a_stack — asymptotics, monotonicity in k_f, and the k_f = 1 identity against the isotropic assembly, bit for bit

round_4_the_same_defect_in_the_productio._doc: The static field path and the torque path have their own loops.  Measured at the preset's stored operating point (43.84 A, 13000 rpm, gamma 10 deg), not assumed.

static_field_path.who: fem_field2d / solve_field2d_on_mesh -> solve_magnetostatics (P1); solve_magnetostatics_fem (P1/P2) is the same three lines
static_field_path.verdict: SAME DEFECT — not converged, 8-9 % low in the gap

no_load._doc: solve_magnetostatics (P1) and solve_magnetostatics_fem (P1/P2) on the mirrored full-ring cross-section at I = 0. The spoke rotor's bridges are already saturated with no current at all, which is why the no-load case is a real test. The LOADED case is in loaded_static.json (this mesh carries no coil regions, so the loaded rows produced here were duplicates and have been removed).

torque_path.verdict: CLEAN — it does not rely on the Picard
torque_path.how_it_solves: a pointwise NEWTON on the field residual to 1e-7, with the damped Picard only as a seed and a fallback.  A Newton-converged A satisfies K(nu(|B(A)|)) A = f, which IS the constitutive law, so its field residual bounds the constitutive residual.

round_4_the_same_defect_in_the_productio.proposed_fix: scratchpad/fem_solver_2d_picard.patch — geometric damping in log(nu), adaptive step, constitutive-residual stop, cap raised 8 -> 60, and a loud warning when the fixed point is not reached.  Verified on a patched COPY: 1.51952 T in 62 sweeps at residual 9.3e-4, against the shipped 1.38472 T on the same problem.  NOT committed — fem_solver_2d is change-controlled.

l_stack_curve_note: ISOTROPIC iron and the OLD (unconverged) 2D leg — every k_flux in these rows is stale by the two corrections in consistency_investigation round 4. k_flux_self is the isotropic model's; the laminated model moves it by -1.6 %.

stage_b._summary: Blockers 1, 2 and 3 are closed and measured, and the sliding band is proven exact (stage_b.sliding_band.proofs).  TASK 46 settles the torque FUNCTIONAL question the previous pass left open and runs the two Stage B studies that were implemented but never executed.  SETTLED: the honest torque of a PM machine is the CO-ENERGY derivative dW'/dtheta at constant current.  The flux-linkage expression 1/2 sum_ph i_ph dpsi_ph/dtheta is a DIFFERENT functional - it keeps the reluctance term whole, keeps half the PM alignment term and drops the magnet's own co-energy - and the magnets-OFF identity proves both implementations are nevertheless correct, agreeing to 5e-11 N.m on a 3e-2 N.m torque.  MEASURED: the end-winding leakage sweep (the end turns add under 0.5 % of the phase inductance) and the long-stack honesty test, which passes and in passing delivers the INDUCTIVE end-effect factor k_L = 1.065 the project has never had.  STILL NOT DELIVERED: a k_T from the co-energy central difference, which needs two more converged nonlinear rotor positions.  The k_T that IS quoted (0.9645) is method-matched, and its method error is now bounded at 0.4 % rather than merely flagged.

machine.materials_note: config/motor_config.yaml is LIVE and its magnet assignment has moved to F52SH_120C since Stage A was measured.  Every number here was produced with the Stage A magnet (F45SH_120C) pinned IN-PROCESS - no file was written and the running backend was not touched - so it is comparable with the Stage A passport above.  A Stage B run that took the live assignment would be a different machine.  tests/test_static3d_stage_b.py pins Br = 1.19 T so this cannot drift silently.

operating_point.daxis_source: fem_solver_2d._resolve_daxis_shift - auto-calibrated per topology, 60.0009 deg for this 12s/14p winding, NOT the legacy 108 deg constant

winding_model.formulation: source field T = Psi(r,theta)*beta(z)*e_r,  curl(T) = J,  assembled as integral(T . curl v)
winding_model.beta: cosine: 1 inside the stack, 0.5*(1+cos(pi*u)) across the end-winding band, u = (|z|-L/2)/h_ew

load_consistency._doc: Blocker 1, as two numbers on ONE mesh and ONE physics: the thick-solenoid benchmark (tube_in_box, 134697 tets, 161864 edge dofs), solved once with the current assembled as integral(J.v) and once as integral(T.curl v) with curl(T) = J.  The question is not whose residual is smaller.  It is whether the Helmholtz projection had anything to take: whatever it takes is the part of the load no magnetostatic field can satisfy, and for an extruded slot current that part IS the missing end turns.

J_source.verdict: 0.39 % of the load vector was deleted before solving, silently

T_source.verdict: EXACTLY zero removed â€” curl(grad psi) vanishes identically in the Nedelec space, so the load is in the operator's range by construction and not by tolerance

held_across_refinement._doc: the T source's consistency is a property of the weak form, not of the mesh

load_consistency.gauge_independence: the same numbers for gauge='tree' (direct) and gauge='none' (CG): 5-6 CG iterations with the regularised-mass preconditioner

winding_validation._doc: Blocker 1's other half: the winding model put against an EXACT solution before it is trusted on a motor.  exact.thick_solenoid_axis_Bz is the field of the source ACTUALLY discretised (an annulus of finite thickness), so the error below is solver error and not a modelling gap.  Lowest-order Nedelec: B = curl(A) is piecewise CONSTANT, so first order is the expected rate and is what is seen.
winding_validation.source: winding3d.solenoid_T â€” T = J*(r_outer - clamp(r, r_i, r_o)) e_z inside |z| < L/2

J_source_on_the_same_mesh.note: the J source is MORE accurate here, and the reason is geometric rather than formulational: this solenoid's J is confined to a conformally meshed tube, while its T is nonzero across the whole bore and is interpolated on coarse air elements.  The motor winding's T is supported only in the copper's radial band, which is the well-resolved part of that cross-section.  The trade is stated because it is real: T buys exact consistency and pays a little interpolation.

iron_anisotropy._doc: Blocker 2: nedelec.py used to REFUSE a laminated Region rather than solve it as solid iron.  It now assembles the diagonal nu = diag(nu_t, nu_t, nu_z) with nu_z derived from solver.axial_mu â€” one homogenisation, inverted, never re-derived.

kf_1_identity._doc: the solid material must be a MEMBER of the lamination family, not a special case: forcing the anisotropic branch at k_f = 1 must reproduce the isotropic assembly

direction_signature._doc: the test that separates the correct tensor from the transposed one â€” a swapped nu converges just as happily and gets both signs backwards.  Magnetised sphere in an iron shell, k_f = 0.92 against solid, A-formulation.
direction_signature.reading: blocking the axial path keeps MORE of a transversely magnetised body's flux in the sheet plane and lets LESS of an axially magnetised one's cross the stack

cross_formulation._doc: scalar P2 vs A/N0 on the RATIO laminated/solid, where the two elements' very different iron errors cancel.  benchmarks.iron_ladder already measured N0 ~6x less accurate than P2 inside iron, so an absolute comparison there measures the element.

M_in_plane.note: the axial columns are ratios of quantities that are zero by symmetry for an in-plane magnet and carry no signal

cross_formulation.verdict: on the quantities with signal the two formulations agree on what lamination does to 0.003-0.25 %, inside the round-4 mesh bracket (~0.6 %)

end_winding_leakage._doc: what the 3D model sees that 2D cannot, as a split of ONE integral rather than a comparison of two models.  lambda = integral(T_1 . B) over the whole machine; split it at the stack-end plane and the inside part is what a 2D cross-section-times-a-length can represent, while the outside part - the axial fringing of the stack field PLUS the end turns' own flux - is invisible to 2D by construction.  The stack end is a mesh plane, so the split is exact and not approximate.
end_winding_leakage.machinery_is_in_place: loaded.unit_phase_windings + loaded.flux_linkage_axial_split + loaded.inductance_matrix; the identity they rest on (integral(T.B) == A^T f == integral(B.H) on a linear problem) is pinned by tests/test_static3d_stage_b.py::test_flux_linkage_from_T_equals_the_stored_energy_identity
end_winding_leakage.how_to_run: one phase at 1 A, magnets OFF, LINEAR iron (an inductance is a derivative and lambda/i on saturating iron is not one), over h_ew = 1.4 / 2.8 / 5.6 mm and over ew_shape cosine/linear, so the end-turn geometry's own influence is measured rather than assumed.
end_winding_leakage.end_winding_factor_note: the project's end_winding_factor = 1.406 for this preset is a RESISTANCE length factor.  The rows in `measured` are the INDUCTIVE counterpart it has never had, and the answer is that the two are not comparable quantities: the end TURNS add under 0.5 % of the phase inductance, while the inductive end effect that does exist for this machine is +6.5 % and lives INSIDE the stack near the end faces (long_stack_honesty_test.the_inductive_end_effect_factor).  The user's ANSYS comparison (1.76 vs auto 1.41) is about copper LENGTH and this study neither confirms nor contradicts it - it measures a different thing, and that is the finding.

measured_under_load_at_the_operating_poi._doc: not the inductance study (that needs magnets off, 1 A and linear iron, and did not get the machine) — this is the SAME split of the same integral on the converged loaded solve, so it is the end fraction of the TOTAL phase linkage at the operating point, magnets included.
measured_under_load_at_the_operating_poi.reading: phase A links 8.637e-4 Wb in total, of which 2.500e-6 Wb (0.289 %) lives beyond the end of the stack.  That is the part no 2D model can represent at all.

measured._doc: Blocker 1's payoff, RUN.  One phase at 1 A, magnets OFF, LINEAR iron - an inductance is a derivative and lambda/i on saturating iron is not one.  L_end is the part of the phase's own linkage that lives beyond the end of the stack: the axial fringing of the stack field PLUS the end turns' own flux, which is exactly what a 2D cross-section-times-a-length cannot represent.  The stack end is a mesh plane, so the split is exact rather than approximate.

axial_resolution_check._doc: every axial layer count DOUBLED (n_stack 5->8, n_ew 4->8, n_cap 6->8) on the same cross-section.  Asked because the h_ew = 1.4 mm rows come out NEGATIVE at the 0.01-0.05 % level, and a sign that is under the resolution of the split would be an artefact rather than a result.
axial_resolution_check.verdict: L_end moves by at most 6 % (0.1317 -> 0.1261 uH at h_ew = 5.6, 0.02864 -> 0.02770 at 2.8) and the NEGATIVE rows stay negative at the same size.  The sign is resolved.  L_self itself is the less converged of the two, moving 0.3-0.6 %.

measured.reading: At the project's own h_ew = tooth_width/2 + wire_width/2 = 2.8 mm, the phase self-inductance is 26.42 uH and the part of it living BEYOND the end of the stack is 0.0286 uH - 0.11 %.  Over a 4x sweep of the end-turn height it goes from -0.0039 uH (-0.015 %, i.e. slightly NEGATIVE: for a short tooth end turn the axial fringing of the stack's own field, which subtracts here, is as large as the end turn's added flux) to +0.1317 uH (+0.50 %) at 5.6 mm, and the cosine and linear beta profiles differ by a factor of 2-3 on that small quantity while both stay under 0.5 %.  The mutuals (M_BA 0.344 uH, M_CA 0.229 uH) do not move with h_ew at all.  So the ANSWER to the question this study was commissioned for - what does the end winding add to the inductance - is: for this tooth-wound machine, under half a percent, against a RESISTANCE end-winding factor of 1.41-1.76.  The end turns cost copper length and almost no inductance.  What they do NOT explain is the 6.3 % inductive end effect the long-stack test finds, which is inside the stack - see stage_b.long_stack_honesty_test.

long_stack_honesty_test._doc: the torque form of this test needs blocker 3.  The form that a single rotor position CAN answer is the INDUCTANCE one: L_end lives in the air above the stack and is geometric, so at 4x stack it must barely move while L_stack scales with the stack and the end FRACTION falls like 1/L.  A split that failed that would not be measuring an end effect at all.
long_stack_honesty_test.how_to_run: three solves at stack_mm 12 / 24 / 48, one phase at 1 A, magnets off, linear iron, same cross-section mesh and the same h_ew = 2.8 mm band; compare L_stack/stack_mm (must be constant) against L_end (must be constant) - loaded.flux_linkage_axial_split returns both.

the_inductive_end_effect_factor._doc: what the honesty test turned out to MEASURE, not just to check.  L_stack/L is not constant - it falls by 4.6 % from 1x to 4x stack - and it falls as a TEXTBOOK 1/L: the two successive differences are -0.06560 and -0.03275 uH/mm, a ratio of 0.4993 against the 0.5 a 1/L law demands, and the two-parameter fit a + b/L reproduces all three rows to 2e-5 uH/mm.  So a is the L -> infinity (i.e. 2D) per-unit-length inductance and b/L is the end effect.
the_inductive_end_effect_factor.reading: the 12 mm machine's phase self-inductance is 6.46 % above what an infinite stack of the same cross-section would give per unit length (k_L = 1.0646).  Of that end effect, only 1.8 % lives BEYOND the stack-end plane; the rest is inside the stack, near the end faces, where the field is not the 2D one.  That is the INDUCTIVE counterpart of the project's end_winding_factor (1.406), which is a RESISTANCE length factor and says nothing about this.

measured._doc: the inductance form, RUN: stack 12 / 24 / 48 mm, one phase at 1 A, magnets off, linear iron, the SAME cross-section mesh and the same h_ew = 2.8 mm band.  L_end lives in the air above the stack and is geometric, so it must barely move; L_stack must scale with the stack, so L_stack/L must be constant and the end FRACTION must fall like 1/L.

demag_under_load._doc: H . M_hat inside the magnets, per axial slice; negative is demagnetising.  The loaded and no-load rows are the SAME mesh and the SAME (linear) iron, so the difference between them is the armature field and nothing else.  LINEAR iron is a stated limitation, not a convenience: this spoke rotor's bridges saturate at I = 0 already, so the absolute levels are not Stage A's nonlinear ones and a converged nonlinear loaded run would move them.

loaded_linear_iron.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising.  At I = 0 the end slice is LESS negative than the mid-plane one (the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet); under load the armature field adds to that, and the two do not have to have the same sign

no_load_linear_iron_same_mesh.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising.  At I = 0 the end slice is LESS negative than the mid-plane one (the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet); under load the armature field adds to that, and the two do not have to have the same sign

nonlinear_loaded_capped.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising.  At I = 0 the end slice is LESS negative than the mid-plane one (the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet); under load the armature field adds to that, and the two do not have to have the same sign

stage_a_no_load_for_contrast._doc: from the Stage A block above: CONVERGED nonlinear, but a different (finer) mesh and ISOTROPIC iron, so this is a contrast and not a subtraction.

demag_under_load.reading: Two statements, and they point opposite ways, which is why both are reported.  ON THE VOLUME MEAN the end slice is the SAFER one and load makes it safer still: the end-vs-mid mean shift goes from +5.5 kA/m at I = 0 (Stage A) to +60.6 kA/m under load.  AT THE WORST ELEMENT the end slice is the more exposed one at I = 0 already (-141.9 kA/m) and stays so under load (-91.8 kA/m) - the armature field does not rescue the corner, it just raises the whole level: the mid-plane worst goes from -616 kA/m to -976 kA/m and the end worst from -758 kA/m to -1068 kA/m.  So load costs this machine roughly 300 kA/m of margin everywhere, and the end region remains the place the worst element lives.  The nonlinear loaded state behind those numbers is NOT converged (constitutive residual 0.164 after 14 capped sweeps), so treat the loaded absolutes as indicative and the SIGNS and ORDER as the result.

nonlinear_loaded_CONVERGED.note: negative H.Mhat is demagnetising.  At I = 0 the end slice is LESS negative than the mid-plane one (the end flux spills into air instead of being pushed back through the magnet); under load the armature field adds to that, and the two do not have to have the same sign
nonlinear_loaded_CONVERGED._doc: H . M_hat inside the magnets per axial slice, on a CONVERGED nonlinear loaded state (52 Picard sweeps, residual 2.746e-3) — the Stage B block below reported this at the sweep cap with a residual of 0.164 and said to treat the absolutes as indicative.  These are the absolutes.

vs_the_capped_state.reading: Converging moved the MID-plane worst element from -976 to -1033 kA/m (5.8 % more exposed) and the END worst from -1068 to -1049 kA/m (1.8 % less), so the end-vs-mid worst SHIFT collapses from -91.8 kA/m to -16.5 kA/m.  The volume means barely move (-425 kA/m mid either way; end -364 -> -358).  The SIGNS and the ORDER that the capped state reported survive — the end slice is still the more exposed one at the worst element and the safer one on the mean — but the magnitude of the end-vs-mid gap does not, which is exactly why the capped state was labelled indicative.  Mesh: 127908 tets at h_gap 0.55 / h_solid 1.70, laminated iron.

nonlinear_cost._doc: the LOADED nonlinear A-formulation solve, cold-started from the linear permeability.  Capped at 14 sweeps ON PURPOSE and it did NOT converge.  The trace is recorded because the cost of converging it is the number Stage B planning actually needs.
nonlinear_cost.comparison: Stage A's SCALAR no-load solve of the same machine needed 58 sweeps to reach 2.9e-3 at the same damping, so the sweep COUNT is the machine's, not the formulation's.  What the A-formulation changes is the price of a sweep: ~75 s at 198834 edge dofs, because every sweep refactorises the regularised-mass preconditioner.
nonlinear_cost.implication: a converged loaded nonlinear 3D solve is of order an hour per rotor position at this mesh, so the energy-method torque - two or three positions per operating point - needs warm-starting from the previous angle (mu_init already exists in both drivers) before it is affordable.

cost._doc: What a loaded 3D solve costs, measured. Mesh: the my_40mm_last cross-section at h_gap 0.55 / h_solid 1.70 mm (3655 triangles), extruded on n_stack 5 + n_ew 4 + n_cap 6 axial layers with the stack end and the end-winding band both on mesh planes. Lowest-order Nedelec, so dofs = edges. MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 throughout, sequential, on a machine the user was also using.

rows.label: loaded, NONLINEAR iron, capped at 14 Picard sweeps (NOT converged)
rows.note: assemble_s/solve_s are the FINAL sweep only; wall_s is the whole Picard. ~44 s of solve per sweep on a quiet machine, ~75 s per sweep wall including the preconditioner refactorisation.

reading: the closed winding costs NOTHING in consistency: source_residual is 0.0 and the Helmholtz projection removes 0.0 on the real cross-section, exactly as on the benchmark
a LINEAR loaded solve is ~76 s at 198834 edge dofs and 24 CG iterations - the regularised-mass preconditioner is doing its job (Stage A measured 17348 Jacobi iterations against 17 with it)
the NONLINEAR loaded solve is the expensive one and it is the Picard, not the linear algebra: 14 sweeps for 613 s and still at a constitutive residual of 0.164

benchmark_costs_for_scale.label: thick solenoid, T source, gauge=none (CG, 5 it)
thick solenoid, J source, gauge=none (CG, 6 it)

torque.status: PARTIAL - the sliding band is proven, the torque FUNCTIONAL question is SETTLED (see functional_settlement: the co-energy derivative is the torque, the flux-linkage functional is blind to the magnet term), and one CONVERGED nonlinear rotor position exists.  The nonlinear co-energy CENTRAL DIFFERENCE still does not, so no k_T is quoted from the energy-difference route.
torque._doc: Torque here is by the ENERGY METHOD only: T = dW'/dtheta at constant current, differenced over the sliding band's own legal angles so the two states sit on bit-identical meshes.  Maxwell stress appears nowhere.  torque3d.co_energy builds W' from the co-energy DENSITY, reading saturable iron off the same B-H curve the Picard converged on (1/2 nu |B|^2 with the frozen permeability is the co-energy of a different, linear material and on a saturated bridge differs by tens of percent).

mesh.note: box_factor 2.5 (r_box = z_box = 50 mm) rather than Stage A's 160 mm: torque is a gap quantity and the truncation bracket Stage A measured (0.008 % on k_flux) is not the limiting error here

converged_position.what_it_took: 52 damped-Picard sweeps to a constitutive residual of 2.746e-3 against a 3e-3 tolerance, 2660 s at 161964 edge dofs on a machine the user was also using.  The Stage B pass stopped at 14 sweeps and 0.164 and EXTRAPOLATED 33; the measured answer is 52.

two_d.who: em_transient_eval -> fem_transient_sliding_band, P2, Newton-converged (picard_resid_max 9.65e-8, no unconverged and no fallback frames)
two_d.method: sb_postproc.hybrid_torque's energy mean <T> = (3/2) p n_par <psi_al i_be - psi_be i_al>

torque.k_T_reading: The number that CAN be quoted is method-matched: the 2D leg's T_avg is itself the flux-linkage/energy mean, and torque3d.dq_torque applies the SAME functional to the 3D flux linkages (loaded.flux_linkage, which is the identity lambda = integral(T_1 . B) the Stage B suite already pins).  It gives T_3d = 0.56551 N.m against T_2d = 0.58631 N.m, i.e. k_T = 0.9645.  Two caveats and both matter: the 3D value is INSTANTANEOUS at rotor_angle 0 while the 2D value is a period MEAN, and the alpha-beta functional is winding-filtered, so the two agree on the mean and not frame by frame.  For scale, k_flux (Stage A, no load) is 0.9517 / 0.9594, so 0.9645 sits where an end-effect ratio should.  [TASK 46] The 'winding-filtered / agrees on the mean and not frame by frame' caveat is now quantified rather than asserted: on this machine the instantaneous expression is 0.35 % from its own period mean at rotor_angle 0 and never more than 0.90 % anywhere in the cycle (functional_settlement.how_wrong_the_instantaneous_dq_IS_on_the_real_machine).  What the same settlement also shows is that the expression is NOT a torque at all in general - on the linear machine it misses by 10x and by sign - so k_T = 0.9645 is a method-matched RATIO and must never be quoted as a virtual-work result.

linear_iron_delta_sweep._doc: the delta sweep the energy method needs, done on the LINEAR machine because it is cheap.  It is NOT a torque of this machine — with linear iron at mu_r 4600 the rotor bridges short the magnet flux and the torque collapses — it is there to show the central difference's behaviour against the angular step.
linear_iron_delta_sweep.RESOLVED: The factor of ten is explained and measured: see stage_b.torque.functional_settlement.  The co-energy central difference IS the torque; the flux-linkage expression is a different functional that misses the magnet's own co-energy and half of the PM alignment term, and on this machine those two omissions are larger than the torque and cancel against the term it does keep.

what_is_missing_and_why: the nonlinear co-energy CENTRAL DIFFERENCE, and it is the only thing between this module and a virtual-work k_T.  One converged rotor position costs 52 Picard sweeps and 44 minutes at this mesh (converged_position); the second and third have never finished.  Warm-starting works and saves 30-40 % (warm_start), which is not enough on a shared box.

a nonlinear magnet-only COGGING sweep, which is what would show the physical cogging line the linear sweep cannot resolve.  Its price is measured and recorded in sliding_band.noise_floor.nonlinear_cogging_sweep (~4.5 hours warm-started at this mesh); nothing blocks it but CPU.

[TASK 46, DONE] the end-winding leakage rows and the long-stack honesty test - both were queued here and both have now been run; see stage_b.end_winding_leakage.measured and stage_b.long_stack_honesty_test.measured.
[TASK 46, DONE] the functional disagreement itself - see stage_b.torque.functional_settlement.

functional_settlement._doc: WHICH functional is the torque, settled by measurement.  Three expressions were in play and only one of them is a torque.  The weak form gives, exactly and on the discrete solution, W' = 1/2 int((Hc + T).B) = W_Hc + W_T with W_Hc = 1/2 int(Hc.B) and W_T = 1/2 sum_ph i_ph psi_ph, psi_ph = int(T_1ph.B) = loaded.flux_linkage.  Splitting B into its magnet and armature parts and using reciprocity, W_Hc = W'_magnet_alone + 1/2 sum i psi_pm and W_T = 1/2 sum i psi_pm + 1/2 i^T L i.  So the WINDING functional keeps the whole reluctance term, keeps exactly HALF of the PM alignment term, and misses the magnet's own co-energy entirely.  It is not an approximation to the torque; it is a different functional with the same units.
functional_settlement.the_discriminating_measurement: magnets OFF, LINEAR iron.  With M = 0 the Hc term vanishes and W' = W_T POINTWISE, so dW'/dtheta and 1/2 sum_ph i_ph dpsi_ph/dtheta are one number from one set of solves.  Any difference there would be an implementation error in torque3d.co_energy or in loaded.flux_linkage and nothing else.

the_three_terms._doc: the torque of the LINEAR machine split into the three terms it is made of.  Superposition is legal here and only here - the iron is LINEAR, so psi_pm = psi(magnets on) - psi(magnets off) is exact.  W' = W'_mm(theta) + sum_ph i_ph psi_pm,ph(theta) + 1/2 i^T L(theta) i, so T = dW'_mm/dtheta [cogging] + sum i dpsi_pm/dtheta [PM alignment] + 1/2 i^T dL/dtheta i [reluctance].
the_three_terms.reading: At a 2.14 deg step: reluctance -3.061574e-02, PM alignment +3.252629e-02, cogging -5.35e-07 N.m, summing to +1.910016e-03 against the co-energy derivative's +1.910016e-03 - they close to 4.6e-12 N.m.  The WINDING functional is reluctance + HALF the alignment = -1.435260e-02: the two largest terms in this machine are the reluctance and the alignment, they are within 6 % of each other and OPPOSITE in sign, so dropping half of one of them does not perturb the answer, it replaces it.  The cogging term is 5.4e-07 N.m, which is under the band's own 2.6e-5 N.m noise floor and is consistent with the linear machine having no resolvable cogging at all.
the_three_terms.and_dq_torque: the magnets-OFF row is the cleanest statement about dq_torque: there the true torque is PURE reluctance, -3.061574e-02 N.m by both honest routes, while the instantaneous (3/2) p (psi_al i_be - psi_be i_al) reads -9.982845e-03 - a third of it, with no magnet anywhere in the problem.  That is what a fundamental-only, winding-filtered mean identity does to a 12s/14p concentrated winding when it is evaluated at one instant.

the_ten_fold_disagreement_explained._doc: the very sweep the Stage B pass recorded as UNRESOLVED, re-read with the SAME solves' flux linkages.  n_ring 336, h_gap 0.55 / h_solid 1.70, box 2.5, n_ew 2, 116280 tets, LINEAR iron, magnets ON, the Stage B operating point.
the_ten_fold_disagreement_explained.reading: at a 2.14 deg step the torque is dW'/dtheta = 1.860e-03 N.m, the winding functional is -1.436e-02 and the magnet term it cannot see is 1.622e-02.  The two large terms very nearly cancel, so the winding functional alone is wrong by an order of magnitude AND by sign.  That is the whole of the factor of ten.

how_wrong_the_instantaneous_dq_IS_on_the._doc: the linear machine says the instantaneous dq expression is not a torque; it does NOT say how big the error is on the machine k_T is actually quoted for.  That is measurable without any new 3D work: the 2D transient already solves every frame of the real, NONLINEAR machine at this operating point, so its own psi and i series read back through the same formula give the instantaneous value frame by frame against the mean hybrid_torque reports.  Stage A materials pinned in-process (F45SH_120C), P2, Newton-converged (field residual 9.6e-8).
how_wrong_the_instantaneous_dq_IS_on_the.reading: On the REAL machine the instantaneous expression swings 1.61 % peak-to-peak about its own mean, the worst frame is 0.90 % off it, and at rotor_angle 0 - the angle the 3D solve sits at - it is -0.35 % off.  So the method error k_T = 0.9645 inherits from evaluating a MEAN identity at one instant is of order 0.4 % and bounded by 0.9 %, not the order of magnitude the linear machine shows.  The reason the two are so different is the physics, not the formula: on the linear machine the reluctance and alignment terms are 16x the net torque and nearly cancel, so any functional error is enormous relative to what is left; on the saturated machine the bridges stop shorting the magnet, the alignment term dominates and the machine behaves like the sinusoidal one the expression assumes.  This bounds the 2D leg's instantaneous error directly and the 3D leg's by inheritance - same machine, same winding filter - which is an assumption and is stated as one.

functional_settlement.what_this_means_for_k_T: The honest torque of a PM machine is the CO-ENERGY derivative dW'/dtheta at constant current, and it is the only torque this module reports.  dq_torque is a third expression again: sb_postproc.hybrid_torque states it is the air-gap power balance P = T omega, whose virtual-work identity holds for the MEAN over an electrical period with the currents rotating with the rotor.  Evaluated at ONE rotor angle with the currents frozen it is not that mean: on the linear machine it swings from -0.040 to +0.081 N.m over 7 ring pitches while the true torque stays near +1.9e-3.  The k_T = 0.9645 quoted below is therefore method-matched and NOT a virtual-work number; it is the same instantaneous formula applied to both legs, and it carries that caveat.  How big that caveat is has now been MEASURED on the real machine rather than left open: see how_wrong_the_instantaneous_dq_IS_on_the_real_machine - 0.35 % at rotor_angle 0, 0.90 % worst case over the cycle.  k_T = 0.9645 therefore stands, with a stated method error of order 0.4 %, and it is still NOT a virtual-work number: the co-energy central difference that would be one needs two more converged nonlinear rotor positions and remains unpaid.

torque.k_T_note: deliberately null.  k_T_flux_linkage = 0.9645 is the method-matched ratio and is quoted under that name so it can never be mistaken for a virtual-work number; this key stays empty until the co-energy central difference pays for it.

closed_winding.how: simulation/static3d/winding3d.py - the coil is a SOURCE FIELD T = Psi(r,theta)*beta(z)*e_r with curl(T) = J, assembled as integral(T . curl v). Inside the stack (beta = 1) the axial current is exactly fem_solver_2d.build_materials' own J_z = dir*I*n_wires/A_copper; above the stack beta falls from 1 to 0 over h_ew = tooth_width/2 + wire_width/2 = 2.80 mm and the tangential end turn carries the return. Each radius closes its own loop, so div J = 0 is an identity, not a tolerance.
closed_winding.why_the_half_model_is_a_whole_loop: the slot current is EVEN in z and the end-turn current is ODD in z, so B_z = 0 on the z = 0 mirror plane for the loaded machine exactly as for the no-load one. The modelled half is one half of a genuine closed loop; the current that leaves through z = 0 leaves through a Dirichlet boundary whose nodes the discrete-gradient projection has already contracted away, so nothing is absorbed there either.
evidence: load consistency on the solenoid benchmark: 3.10e-16, and the Helmholtz projection removed EXACTLY 0.0 of a load of norm 1.2e4 (a J source on the same mesh: 9.63e-3, and 0.395 % of the load deleted)
load consistency on the REAL 40 mm cross-section under load, 164475 tets / 198834 edge dofs: source_residual = 0.0, removed = 0.0
validated against exact.thick_solenoid_axis_Bz: on-axis L2 2.37 % -> 1.16 % -> 1.07 % over three meshes (lowest-order Nedelec, B piecewise constant, first order)
the winding closes over the 180 deg sector to 5.8e-15 of its own scale, so T is anti-periodic and the sector solve is the machine
the sampled winding delivers the ampere-turns build_materials asked for to 0.0013 % (433.99 At against 434.00)
modelling_choices_stated: the end turn stays at its own radius and crosses tangentially over the tooth in a band above the stack; a real bundle also migrates radially. h_ew and the beta shape are parameters and their effect is measured, not assumed.
the copper outline is not a mesh line (slots are meshed as air, as in Stage A), so the ampere-turns are exact but their sub-slot distribution is resolved only to the element size.

anisotropic_iron_in_the_A_formulation.how: nedelec.py now assembles nu = diag(nu_t, nu_t, nu_z) through _curlcurl_aniso, with nu_z = 1/axial_mu(1/nu_t, k_f) - the scalar solver's own homogenisation, inverted, never re-derived. The Picard reads the B-H curve at the IN-PLANE |B| in a laminated region, the same rule solver.solve_static3d_nonlinear uses. It no longer raises NotImplementedError on a laminated Region.
evidence: k_f = 1 reproduces the isotropic assembly to 4-5e-12 of |A| - the solid material is a member of the family, not a branch
direction signature: laminating raises a transversely magnetised body's iron |B| by +18.8 % and lowers an axially magnetised one's by -24.2 %; a transposed tensor gets both signs backwards
scalar P2 vs A/N0 agree on the lamination RATIO to 0.003 % (gap, in-plane M) and 0.18-0.25 % (gap and magnet interior, axial M), inside the round-4 mesh bracket of ~0.6 %

rotatable_rotor_with_identical_topology.status: SOLVED — see stage_b.sliding_band for the construction and its proofs.  What it was blocking (the energy-method k_T) is only partly delivered; see stage_b.torque.
rotatable_rotor_with_identical_topology.what_is_needed: the energy method needs W'(theta) at two or three rotor angles on a mesh whose CONNECTIVITY does not change, or the mesh difference swamps the torque signal.

design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work._doc: mesher._weld_belt_into_half and p2_projection.SlipProjection do exactly this in 2D and were read in full for this pass. The 3D port is mechanical but not small.
design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work.1_geometry: mesh the cross-section as THREE pieces instead of one: a stator part (r >= r_stator_in), a rotor part (r <= r_rotor_out), and a belt whose two halves each carry a UNIFORM ring of N nodes at the mid-gap radius. The slip is a node identification at that one radius, so no element is ever sheared and the element matrices never change.
design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work.2_rotation: rotation is a RE-LABELLING, not a coordinate change: rotor ring node k is welded to stator ring node k+m. Legal angles are integer multiples of the ring pitch 2*pi/N. Element geometry is bit-identical at every m, which is the whole point.
design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work.3_the_sector: the rotor is 180 deg anti-periodic at ANY rotor angle, so the anti-periodic cut constraint is untouched by rotation. A ring node pushed past theta = 180 deg reappears at theta = 0 carrying a factor bc_sign = -1; the 2D code does this in p2_projection.ring_map and the 3D version needs the same wrap-with-sign.
design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work.4_what_is_genuinely_new_in_3d: the weld is on NEDELEC EDGE dofs, not nodes. The mid-gap cylinder's surface mesh must match under the shift - it does, because both sides are extruded from the same uniform ring on the same z levels and motor_mesh's prism split is already rotation-equivariant - and each welded edge pair carries TWO signs: its own orientation sign, which periodic.edge_dof_pairs already computes, and the anti-periodic wrap sign. The sector constraint and the slip constraint then have to be composed in ONE SIGNED UNION-FIND rather than applied in sequence, because a ring node on the cut plane belongs to both.
design_the_2d_solver_already_proves_work.5_the_proof_it_must_pass: rotate by one full pole pitch: the machine maps onto itself anti-periodically and the co-energy must return bit-identically. Then a magnet-only cogging sweep over many pitches must be smooth, with no sawtooth at the relabelling period.

rotatable_rotor_with_identical_topology.why_it_did_not_land_in_this_pass: the cross-section mesher (motor_mesh.build_section_mesh_2d) produces ONE gmsh mesh of the whole wedge, with a free Delaunay gap. The three-piece build with two uniform rings, the edge-dof weld with two signs, and the composed signed union-find are a rewrite of the meshing and constraint layers, not an addition to them. The two blockers that WERE closed had to come first: without a consistent closed winding and without anisotropic iron, a torque from that band would have been a number produced by a load the projection had partly eaten, in solid iron.
rotatable_rotor_with_identical_topology.cost_note: the 2D band uses n_slip = 1008-1680 nodes per ring. A 3D ring at 180 nodes per 180 deg sector gives a 1 deg pitch, an 0.21 mm arc against the 0.20 mm gap - a sane aspect ratio and a usable delta for a central difference. That sizing is a measurement to make, not an assumption to carry.

sliding_band._doc: Blocker 3, CLOSED.  The cross-section is meshed in TWO pieces cut at the mid-gap radius, both carrying the SAME uniform ring of n_ring vertices; the mesh is deliberately TORN there and stitched by a constraint, so turning the rotor is a re-labelling of which edge dof is welded to which and no node ever moves.  simulation/static3d/band.py + torque3d.py, tests/test_static3d_band.py (17 fast tests, 3 behind STATIC3D_FULL).

construction.pieces: rotor r <= r_mid (iron, magnets, shaft, its half of the gap) | stator r >= r_mid (iron, slots, outer air).  The two share NO node.
construction.ring: a uniform polygon of n_ring vertices at the mid-gap radius handed to gmsh as GEOMETRY POINTS on both pieces, so every one of them is a mesh node; band._ring_nodes refuses the mesh if gmsh put any other node on that circle, which is what would silently give the two pieces different rings
construction.legal_angles: integer multiples of the ring pitch 2 pi / n_ring — at n_ring = 336 that is 1.07143 deg mech and 0.2244 mm of arc against a 0.200 mm gap
construction.weld: the interface is a prismatic surface (ring index k x axial level l) and EVERY edge lying in it is welded: axial (k,l)-(k,l+1), angular (k,l)-(k+1,l) and the quad face DIAGONAL (k,l)-(k+1,l+1).  Welding two of the three leaves the tangential trace discontinuous, i.e. a torn gap that still solves.
construction.diagonals: motor_mesh.extrude_section splits each prism through the lower-KEY end of its base edge, so the two pieces agree on the diagonals only if the ring key is monotone in the ring index on both.  band.ring_split_key does that AND keeps the two radial cut planes' triangulations identical: the ring node is the outermost cut node of the rotor piece and the innermost of the stator piece, so a key above every other key puts it on the same side of its radial neighbour on both planes.
construction.signs: each welded pair carries TWO signs — the anti-periodic WRAP (a ring node pushed past theta = sector re-enters at 0 with bc_sign) and the edge ORIENTATION (scikit-fem orients every edge low-vertex to high, which knows nothing about the rotation).  The sector cut and the slip constraint are composed in ONE signed union-find, because a ring node on a cut plane belongs to both.
construction.wrap_period: ring NODES reduce into [0, Nring-1]; ring CELLS reduce mod Nring-1.  Reducing a cell by its two endpoints instead gives the cell straddling the cut two different signs.
construction.contradiction_gate: a signed union-find silently DROPS a union whose two dofs are already related with the other sign, and a dropped weld is a torn gap with a plausible picture.  SlipWeld.build raises instead, then re-checks every constraint against the classes it produced.  tests/test_static3d_band.py::test_a_wrap_sign_error_is_caught_rather_than_solved corrupts one entry and requires the raise.
construction.gmsh_limits: the ring pitch and h_gap must be within a factor of ~4: finer element size and gmsh subdivides the ring segments (the two pieces stop sharing a ring); coarser and gmsh will not fill the gap from a boundary that much finer than its target size — measured, n_ring = 672 (0.112 mm arc) against h_gap = 0.9 mm did not return in 15 minutes.  Both bounds are checked in build_banded_section.

proof_a_merged_vs_weld._doc: a genuinely CONFORMAL mesh (the two rings identified) against the welded one at zero shift: at zero shift the weld must do exactly what shared nodes would do for free

proof_a2_whole_sector_shift._doc: shifting by the whole sector maps this machine onto itself ANTI-periodically (7 poles per 180 deg is odd), so with the magnets alone the co-energy must return bit-identically; every constraint has been multiplied by bc_sign exactly once

proof_a3_the_mesh_never_moves._doc: element geometry bit-identical at every legal angle

co_energy_two_routes._doc: 1/2 A^T f (the load) vs the volume integral of the co-energy density (the B-H reading of every element) — different inputs, same number on a linear machine

proofs._doc: PROOF A: merging the two rings gives a genuinely CONFORMAL mesh of the same machine, and welding them at zero shift must produce the same discrete problem.  It does, to 1.1e-15 of the co-energy — the weld is not a coupling that happens to be close, it IS the shared-node mesh.  PROOF A2: a whole-sector shift maps this machine onto itself anti-periodically (7 poles per 180 deg is odd), and every constraint in the model has then been multiplied by bc_sign exactly once; the co-energy returns BIT-IDENTICALLY (rel diff 0.0).  PROOF A3: the mesh points and elements are unchanged across shifts and the number of free weld classes does not depend on the angle.

noise_floor._doc: PROOF B, and what it actually measured.  A magnet-only sweep with LINEAR iron over 9 ring pitches.  The physical cogging of this cross-section is NOT resolvable in that state — the unsaturated rotor bridges short ~96 % of the magnet flux, so the gap fundamental is 0.058 T against the saturated machine's 1.47 — and what the sweep sees is therefore almost entirely the band's OWN discretisation bias: the rotor's dofs weld to different parts of an unstructured stator gap mesh at every shift.  That is worth having as a number rather than as a worry, because it is the floor under every torque this construction will report.
noise_floor.reading: the Nyquist bin — a SAWTOOTH at the relabelling period, which is the signature of a mis-weld and which no machine can produce — is not the dominant line (0.25 of the largest).  The absolute floor is ~1.3e-5 N.m, four to five orders below the loaded torque, so it does not limit k_T.  What this sweep does NOT do is show the physical cogging line; that needs nonlinear iron and was not affordable in this pass.

nonlinear_cogging_sweep.status: QUEUED — not affordable in this pass, and here is the price
nonlinear_cogging_sweep._doc: what would show the PHYSICAL cogging line the linear sweep cannot resolve: a magnet-only sweep with NONLINEAR iron over one slot pitch.  The linear sweep above measures the band's own discretisation floor (2.6e-5 N.m) and not cogging, because with unsaturated bridges the gap fundamental is 0.058 T against the saturated machine's 1.47.
nonlinear_cogging_sweep.cost_basis: MEASURED, not guessed: one CONVERGED nonlinear position of this machine is 52 damped-Picard sweeps and 2660 s at 161964 edge dofs (stage_b.torque.converged_position), and warm-starting from the neighbouring angle saves 30-40 % (stage_b.warm_start).  A sweep needs at least 9 positions to resolve a line and its harmonics, so 9 x ~1800 s warm = ~4.5 hours of sustained single-core work, or ~1.5-2 hours on the coarser n_ring = 168 / 55836-tet mesh at a floor that is then the coarse mesh's, not this one's.
nonlinear_cogging_sweep.why_not_now: this pass shared the box with the user's own optimizer; a 4-hour sustained run is not a background task.  Nothing blocks it technically — band + torque3d already do it (the driver's cog stage) — it is purely CPU.

warm_start._doc: Blocker 3's prerequisite: the energy method needs two or three rotor positions and a cold nonlinear loaded position is tens of Picard sweeps, so the previous angle's permeability has to be carried in.

warm.note: not run to convergence — the process was killed at sweep 28 while still descending

warm_start.measured: Warm-starting HALVES the starting point: the first sweep's constitutive residual is 0.369 against the cold start's 0.9997, so the permeability from a rotor position 1.07 deg away really is much closer to the answer.  But the driver then throws part of that away: it starts every solve at damping 0.35, and by sweep 2 the warm solve has OVERSHOT to 0.716 — worse than where it began — after which the adaptive halving has to climb back down.  At sweep 28 it was at 5.6e-3 against the cold solve's 52 sweeps to 2.7e-3, so the saving is real but is roughly 30-40 % rather than the several-fold a warm start should give.

the_fix.what: the first Picard step is scheduled off the residual the solve is actually handed: d = damping * min(1, r_0), floored at d_floor = 0.02.  `damping` stays the caller's cold-start guess, and on a COLD start (r_0 ~ 1) the schedule hands it straight back, so no cold solve in the project moves.  A caller that wants the old fixed behaviour passes damping_init explicitly - which is how the control run below was taken.
the_fix.pinned_by: tests/test_static3d_spike.py::test_a_warm_start_gets_a_first_step_scaled_to_how_warm_it_is - a cold ring keeps the caller's step, a ring warm-started from a NEARBY PHYSICAL solve (95 % magnetisation, r_0 = 0.43 against the cold 0.99) gets a smaller one, the warm run's sweep count is no worse than the same warm start under the old fixed step, and all three land on the same iron to 2 %.

the_fix_measured._doc: the measurement that exposed the defect, repeated with the fix and with the old behaviour as the CONTROL - all three in one process, on one mesh, at one tolerance.  This mesh is NOT the one the defect rows above were taken on (box_factor 2.0, h_gap 0.5, h_solid 2.2 -> 125928 tets / 159496 edge dofs, against the 127908 tets of stage_b.torque.mesh), so read the three rows against each other and not against the cold row above.
the_fix_measured.machine: my_40mm_last, Stage A materials, the Stage B operating point, loaded nonlinear A-formulation on the sliding band

warm_scheduled.note: shift 1 (one ring pitch, 1.0714 deg) from the cold solve's converged mu, first step scheduled to 0.35 * 0.3631 = 0.1271

warm_old_fixed_step.note: THE CONTROL: same warm start, damping_init = 0.35 forced, i.e. the behaviour before this fix

the_fix_measured.reading: Warm-starting is worth 53 -> 40 sweeps on its own, and the scheduled first step is worth a further 40 -> 37.  What the schedule removes is visible in one number: the old first step drives sweep 2 to 0.691 - nearly twice the 0.363 it was HANDED - while the scheduled run never rises above 0.283 and descends monotonically out of the start.  It is worth 3 sweeps and not more because the halving is fast: the overshoot is repaid by sweep 5 and both runs then join the SAME tail, which is where a warm solve's cost really sits (~35 of its 40 sweeps at d ~ 0.04-0.07, set by the stability edge, not by the starting point).  53 -> 40 is therefore all a perfect first step could ever have bought; making the tail cheaper is acceleration or a Newton step, not a damping schedule.

the_answer_is_unmoved.why_it_matters: the two warm runs took different paths (different first step, 37 sweeps against 40) to the same constitutive fixed point, and their co-energies agree to 1.7e-5 relative.  This is a COST change; the physics is untouched.

the_fix_measured.wall_time_is_not_the_metric_here: quoted because it was measured, not because it is comparable: 3211 s for the cold solve's 53 sweeps (61 s/sweep) against 297 s for the scheduled warm solve's 37 (8.0 s/sweep) in the SAME process.  A sweep does not cost the same everywhere - a state far from the fixed point is worse conditioned and its CG works harder, and the first solve in a process pays one-time setup the later ones do not - so the honest comparison between the two WARM runs is sweeps (40 vs 37); their wall times (296 s vs 297 s) are inside that noise.

measured_and_rejected.what: a trust region on the recovery: cap the step at min(1.6 d, damping, 0.7 * d_bad) where d_bad is the smallest step ever seen to increase the residual, so the sawtooth cannot re-climb.
measured_and_rejected.verdict: REJECTED and NOT in the code.  It does suppress the sawtooth - d locks at 0.070 from sweep 16 - but the descent then crawls (1.8e-2 to 6.3e-3 over the next twenty sweeps) and the run takes 40, no better than doing nothing.  The overshoots the cap removes are what push d down to the ~0.035 the tail needs: the ratchet is not fighting the loop, it is searching for the step the tail wants, and freezing it is worse than letting it search.

the_fix_measured.reproduce: one process, one BandedModel (my_40mm_last, Stage A materials, n_ring 336, box_factor 2.0, h_gap 0.5, h_solid 2.2, n_stack 4, n_cap 4, n_ew 3, linear_iron False), then model.solve(0) cold; model.solve(1, mu_init=<its mu_converged>) for the scheduled run; and the same warm call with damping_init=0.35 for the control.  tol 3e-3, max_iter 45, damping 0.35, cg_tol 1e-10.
